title: The wheel of sacrifice
hookLine: food, rain, offering, action, and back again: a wheel the world turns on, and a hard word for anyone who only takes
carry: yajna: offer first, then eat what remains

cards: Breakfast this morning, whatever it was: toast, rice, coffee. Follow it backward. Somebody sold it to you, somebody drove it there, somebody harvested it.
It grew because rain fell and sun shone and someone planted and weeded. And that farmer ate food someone else grew.
Keep going and there's no beginning, just a circle of people and weather and earth, each handing something on. The Gita gave that circle a name.
And it has a very blunt word for anyone who eats from it without handing anything back.

teach.b: Krishna tells a story of the beginning. The creator, Prajapati, brought forth beings together with yajna, sacrifice, offering, and said: by this you'll flourish; let this be your wish-fulfilling cow.
Nourish the gods with it, and the gods will nourish you. Nourishing one another, you'll reach the highest good. Then the blunt word.
Whoever enjoys the gifts given, without offering anything back, is a stena.

teach.h: WHO ONLY TAKES IS A THIEF.
teach.b: A thief. The good who eat what's left after the offering are freed from wrong. But those who cook only for themselves, bhunjate te tv agham papa, eat wrong itself.
Now the wheel. In Sanskrit: annad bhavanti bhutani, parjanyad anna sambhavah, yajnad bhavati parjanyo, yajnah karma samudbhavah. From food, beings come to be.
From rain, food. From sacrifice, rain. And sacrifice is born of action.

Whoever doesn't help turn the wheel set turning like this, Krishna says, lives in vain. In the Vedic world yajna meant fire rituals, offerings poured into the flame; Hindus still perform them, as homa or havan.

But the Gita widens the word as it goes; by chapter four it counts many kinds of work as yajna. So it's the family cooking and first setting some aside for God, or for a guest, or for the cow outside.
It's the practice from camp three, food offered, then shared.
And that's this week: the self never slain, the duty that's yours, the line about the fruit, sthitaprajna, the chain and its end, act anyway, and now yajna, the wheel.
In the Gita's picture, every act is either a turn of the wheel or a theft from it.

how: Many Hindus offer food to God before eating and set a portion aside for guests, animals or those in need; Gita 3.13, on eating what remains after the offering, and 3.14's wheel of food, rain and sacrifice are often cited to explain these customs.

o: a fast kept on holy days
an offering, a gift given back

p: sacrifice, offering, from which rain comes
a thief: one who takes and never gives

games.q: you've cooked a good meal for yourself. according to Gita 3.13, what makes the difference?
o: offering it first, then eating what remains.
games.why: the good eat what's left after the offering. those who cook only for themselves, the verse says, eat wrong itself.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you received today, food, a kindness, a paycheck, warm water, and follow it backward, hand to hand: the driver, the farmer, the rain.
Then look forward and ask who's downstream of you, and what you'll hand on. If you pray, you can offer the day's first bite before you eat it.

wordCard.voice: Yajna. Sacrifice, offering: first the Vedic fire rite, then in the Gita any action given, not grabbed. Food from rain, rain from offering, offering from action.
